newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FTC says it concerned by alcohol ads.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FTC says it concerned by alcohol ads.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission said Wednesday it is concerned about alcoholic beverage advertising, but declined to confirm a report that it has launched a new investigation.

"The whole question of alcoholic beverage advertising is of concern to us," said FTC spokeswoman Victoria Streitfeld. But she declined to comment on a Wall Street Journal report that the FTC had voted to launch an investigation into the issue starting with ads being run by distiller Seagram Co. and by Stroh Brewery Co.
Streitfeld said the FTC generally does not confirm or deny reports of its investigations.

The FTC joins the Federal Communications Commission in expressing concern about advertising of alcohol advertising on television since the distilled spirits industry decided to end a decades-old voluntary ban on television and radio advertising.
The ban had been in place since 1936 for radio and 1948 for television, and major networks CBS, NBC, ABC and Fox have announced they will continue to bar liquor ads from their television stations.
But that left some 1,200 independent stations that could be targeted by liquor companies and FCC Chairman Reed Hundt appealed to them to continue the ban.
President Clinton has also joined the chorus in scolding the industry for dropping its ban.
Seagram Co. has been running ads in selected local markets. The beer and wine industries have had no such voluntary ban and are major television and radio advertisers.
Neither Seagram nor Stroh company officials could immediately be reached for comment on the reported FTC investigation.
The FTC has power to scrutinize advertising for accuracy and fairness, Streitfeld said. In such a case, the agency could consider the content and the placement of ads.
Advertising directed at young people under the legal drinking age of 21 could be considered unfair since they cannot legally buy the product.
